# Tidyup 12: Extended metadata for R package repositories

**Champion**: Gábor Csárdi<br>
**Co-champion**: Aaron Jacobs, Greg Lin<br>
**Status**: Draft

## Abstract

This tidyup specifies a set of files that an R package repository can
serve, in addition to the usual `PACKAGES` files, to describe its full
history: every source package version it ever published, the packages
it removed, and every binary build of every package version. Tools that
lock or reproduce R projects need this information, and today they can
only get it by scraping several services. The format is plain DCF and
TSV, compressed with zstd, so it is easy to produce and easy to read.

Posit Package Manager (P3M) data for CRAN and Bioconductor is
published in this format at `https://ppm.r-pkg.org/v1` and
`https://ppm-bioc.r-pkg.org/v1`. `rig` is the reference client, and uses
these files to solve and lock `rproj.toml` projects, see
[Tidyup 9](009-rproj-toml.md) and [Tidyup 11](011-rproj-lock.md).

## Motivation

- **`PACKAGES` only describes the latest versions.**

  A CRAN-like repository's `PACKAGES` file lists the current version of
  each package. Older versions live in `src/contrib/Archive/`, which
  has no index of its own, so a resolver cannot see their
  dependencies without downloading and unpacking every tarball. A
  dependency solver that may need to go back to an older version, for
  example to satisfy an upper bound, or to reproduce a project as it
  was on a given day, needs all of them.

- **No record of when a version was published.**

  Reproducing a project "as of" a date needs the date each version
  first appeared. `PACKAGES` does not have it. Snapshot repositories
  have it implicitly, one full `PACKAGES` file per day, but finding the
  first snapshot of a version means searching through them.

- **No record of removed packages.**

  CRAN archives packages regularly. A tool cannot tell an archived
  package from a typo, or tell the user when and why it disappeared,
  without the archive date.

- **Binaries are scattered across many `PACKAGES` files.**

  P3M serves binaries for many Linux distributions, macOS and Windows,
  for many R versions, from daily snapshots. Finding out which builds
  exist for a package means asking one `PACKAGES` file per platform, R
  version and date. A lock file that covers several platforms and R
  versions needs all of those answers at once.

- **Binaries depend on the versions they were built against.**

  A binary of a package with `LinkingTo` dependencies includes code
  from the headers of those dependencies. If the installed version of a
  `LinkingTo` dependency differs, the binary may not work. `PACKAGES`
  does not record which versions a binary was built against.

## Solution

A repository with extended metadata has a base URL, and serves these
files under it:

```
<base>/METADATA
<base>/ALLPACKAGES.zst
<base>/ALLPACKAGES
<base>/ARCHIVEDPACKAGES.zst
<base>/ARCHIVEDPACKAGES
<base>/binaries/<package>.tsv.zst
```

The plain text files have the same content as their `.zst` counterparts.
The extended metadata does not replace the repository: package files
are still downloaded from the URLs listed in the metadata, and the
repository may still serve regular `PACKAGES` files for tools that do
not know about this format.

This format is for repositories that keep old package versions and
old binary builds available after they publish new ones. Download
URLs should be stable: the URL of a file should not change, and it
should keep working for as long as the repository serves the file.
This is not required, but it is strongly suggested, because lock
files record these URLs.

The current instances are:

| Repository | Base URL |
|---|---|
| CRAN | `https://ppm.r-pkg.org/v1` |
| Bioconductor release `<v>` | `https://ppm-bioc.r-pkg.org/v1/<v>`, e.g. `https://ppm-bioc.r-pkg.org/v1/3.22` |

### `METADATA`

`METADATA` is a DCF file with a single record that describes the
repository as a whole:

```
Format-Version: 1.0
Generated: 2026-11-24T06:00:00Z
```

Fields:

- `Format-Version`: the version of the format of the extended
  metadata, as `<major>.<minor>`, see [Versioning](#versioning). This
  tidyup describes version 1.0.
- `Generated`: optional, the time the repository last wrote the
  files, in RFC 3339 format.

Readers must ignore fields they do not know.

`METADATA` is small and not compressed, so clients can check the
version before they download the much larger `ALLPACKAGES.zst`.

### `ALLPACKAGES`

`ALLPACKAGES` is a DCF file, in the same format as `PACKAGES`, with one
record for every source package version the repository ever published,
archived or not. For CRAN this is around 200,000 records.

```
Package: cli
Version: 3.6.6
Depends: R (>= 3.4)
Imports: utils
Suggests: callr, covr, crayon, digest, glue (>= 1.6.0), grDevices, htmltools, htmlwidgets, knitr, methods, processx, ps (>= 1.3.4.9000), rlang (>= 1.0.2.9003), rmarkdown, rprojroot, rstudioapi, testthat (>= 3.2.0), tibble, whoami, withr
License: MIT + file LICENSE
NeedsCompilation: yes
SHA256: 27b5e74a6b2a8264457ce8412ded40aa7b660e01894bea4bfde956bbc4b5b294
Id: b2b58d6dd82f5798b335e39c00591686a01fd3e94399ef898e146173e36f18f9
Snapshot: 2026-04-10
DownloadURL: https://p3m.dev/cran/2026-04-10/src/contrib/cli_3.6.6.tar.gz
```

Fields copied from the package's `DESCRIPTION` file, if present:

- `Package`, `Version` (always present).
- `Depends`, `Imports`, `LinkingTo`, `Suggests`, `Enhances`.
- `License`, `License_is_FOSS`, `License_restricts_use`.
- `NeedsCompilation`, `Priority`, `OS_type`, `Archs`,
  `SystemRequirements`.

Fields added by the repository, always present:

- `SHA256`: the SHA-256 hash of the file at `DownloadURL`.
- `Id`: an identifier of the source tarball, in the same format as a
  SHA-256 hash: 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Different
  tarballs must have different ids, and the id of a tarball must not
  change over time. The binary indices use this id as well.

  A repository can use its `SHA256` field as the id. P3M uses the
  SHA-256 hash of the original source tarball, as published by the
  upstream repository (CRAN or Bioconductor).
- `Snapshot`: the date the version first appeared in the repository,
  as `YYYY-MM-DD`.
- `DownloadURL`: the download URL of the source tarball. It should
  be a stable URL, see above. It is one of:
  - a full URL, e.g.
    `https://p3m.dev/cran/2026-04-10/src/contrib/cli_3.6.6.tar.gz`,
  - an absolute path, e.g.
    `/cran/2026-04-10/src/contrib/cli_3.6.6.tar.gz`, or
  - a relative path, e.g. `2026-04-10/src/contrib/cli_3.6.6.tar.gz`.

  Readers resolve a path against the URL of the file that contains
  it, as in RFC 3986: an absolute path keeps the scheme and host of
  that URL, and a relative path may use `../`. Paths let a repository
  work behind any host name, and relative paths also behind any proxy
  path.

Fields added by the repository, if they apply to the version:

- `Blocked`: set if the repository blocks the version, i.e. it
  refuses to serve it, no matter how old it is. The value is the kind
  of rule that blocks it: `package`, `license`, `vulnerability` or
  `deleted`. Readers must accept other values as well.
- `BlockedRule`: an identifier of the rule that blocks the version.
  Its format is up to the repository.
- `BlockedReason`: a description of the rule that blocks the version,
  for people.
- `BlockedUntil`: set if the version is blocked because it is too new,
  e.g. a rule blocks versions younger than seven days. It is the time
  the version becomes available, in RFC 3339 format, e.g.
  `2026-04-17T00:00:00Z`. Readers compare it to the current time; the
  version is blocked before it. A version may have both `Blocked` and
  `BlockedUntil`, then it stays blocked after `BlockedUntil`.
- `Vulnerabilities`: the known vulnerabilities of the version, as a
  comma-separated list, sorted by id. Each item is a vulnerability id,
  followed by its highest CVSS base score in parentheses, if it has
  one, e.g. `CVE-2024-27322 (8.8), GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx`.
- `Yanked`: set if the version is yanked, see
  [Yanked versions and builds](#yanked-versions-and-builds). The value
  is the time of the yank, in RFC 3339 format, e.g.
  `2026-11-20T10:00:00Z`.
- `YankedReason`: a description of why the version was yanked, for
  people.

These fields describe the repository's policy when it wrote the file.
A version without them may still be blocked when it is downloaded, if
the repository's rules changed since.

Optional fields added by the repository:

- `Published`: the time the version was published by the upstream
  repository, in the same format as the `Published` field of CRAN
  packages, i.e. `YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss UTC`, e.g.
  `2026-05-27 07:50:09 UTC`.
- `Filesize`: the size of the file at `DownloadURL`, in bytes, as an
  integer, e.g. `26267`.

The repository may add other fields as well, e.g. other fields from
the package's `DESCRIPTION` file. Readers must ignore the fields they
do not know.

Rules for readers:

- Records are in no particular order.

- The same `(Package, Version)` pair may appear more than once. This
  happens when the upstream repository replaced a tarball without
  changing its version number. The records differ in `SHA256`,
  `Id`, `Snapshot` and `DownloadURL`, and possibly in the
  other fields. There are about 350 such pairs for CRAN. Each of these
  records is valid, and readers may use any of them.

- The file may have comment lines, starting with `#`. Readers must
  skip them. The first line of the file should be a comment with the
  format version, see [Versioning](#versioning):

  ```
  # Format-Version: 1.0
  ```

- Some records may have dependency fields that do not parse, e.g.
  `Depends: tcltk (butonlyfortheGUI), allotherfunctionsarestandalone)`.
  Readers should skip these records, not the whole file.

### `ARCHIVEDPACKAGES`

`ARCHIVEDPACKAGES` lists the packages that the upstream repository
removed. It has the same format and the same fields as `ALLPACKAGES`,
plus one more field:

- `Archived`: the date the package was archived, as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

There is one record per archived package, describing the last version
published before it was archived.

```
Package: gpclib
Version: 1.5-6
Depends: R (>= 3.0.0), methods
Imports: graphics
License: file LICENSE
License_restricts_use: yes
NeedsCompilation: yes
SHA256: 5ef1de6f69ca88b8d9960b3c637d566b59d7401aa4ec1d3dc30bb248e9126c00
Id: fa4e3e1f74e327b185e873052f826312ed6f71cc907a49be4c1e224ace7b5286
Snapshot: 2020-03-02
DownloadURL: https://p3m.dev/cran/2020-03-02/src/contrib/gpclib_1.5-6.tar.gz
Archived: 2023-04-06
```

A package is "current" if it has a record in `ALLPACKAGES` and does
not have one in `ARCHIVEDPACKAGES`. If an archived package comes back
to the upstream repository, the repository removes its record from
`ARCHIVEDPACKAGES`.

### `binaries/<package>.tsv.zst`

There is one binary index per package, a zstd-compressed,
tab-separated file. It may start with comment lines, starting with
`#`, the first of which should give the format version, see
[Versioning](#versioning). The next line is a header with the column
names, and each other line is one downloadable file: the source
tarball or a binary build.

```
# Format-Version: 1.0
package version platform                                 r_version source-id url                                                                                     linkingto
cli     3.6.6   source                                   *         b2b58d…   https://p3m.dev/cran/2026-04-10/src/contrib/cli_3.6.6.tar.gz
cli     3.6.6   aarch64-apple-darwin                     4.6       b2b58d…   https://p3m.dev/cran/2026-04-10/bin/macosx/sonoma-arm64/contrib/4.6/cli_3.6.6.tgz
cli     3.6.6   x86_64-w64-mingw32                       4.6       b2b58d…   https://p3m.dev/cran/2026-04-10/bin/windows/contrib/4.6/cli_3.6.6.zip
cli     3.6.6   x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-ubuntu-24.04    4.6       b2b58d…   https://p3m.dev/cran/2026-04-10/bin/linux/noble-x86_64/4.6/src/contrib/cli_3.6.6.tar.gz
cli     3.6.6   aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu-manylinux_2_28 4.6       b2b58d…   https://p3m.dev/cran/2026-04-10/bin/linux/manylinux_2_28-arm64/4.6/src/contrib/cli_3.6.6.tar.gz
```

Columns:

- `package`: the package name.
- `version`: the package version, exactly as in `ALLPACKAGES`.
- `platform`: `source` for the source tarball, otherwise the platform
  the binary was built for, see [Platforms](#platforms), e.g.
  `aarch64-apple-darwin` or `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-ubuntu-24.04`.
- `r_version`: `*` for source tarballs, otherwise the minor R version
  the binary was built for, e.g. `4.5`.
- `source-id`: the `Id` of the source tarball of the
  version, from `ALLPACKAGES`. It is the same on every row of a
  version. It is *not* the hash of the file at `url`, so it cannot be
  used to check a download, use `sha256` or `md5` for that. It
  identifies the source tarball the binary was built from.
- `url`: the download URL of the file. It should be a stable URL,
  see above. Like `DownloadURL` in `ALLPACKAGES`, it is a full URL,
  an absolute path or a relative path, resolved against the URL of
  the index. The index is in `binaries/`, so a relative path starts
  with `../` to get to the base URL, e.g.
  `../2026-04-10/bin/windows/contrib/4.6/cli_3.6.6.zip`.
- `sha256`: the SHA-256 hash of the file at `url`.
- `md5`: the MD5 hash of the file at `url`.
- `filesize`: the size of the file at `url`, in bytes, as an integer.
- `built`: `NA` for source tarballs. Otherwise the `Built` field of
  the binary package, in the same format as in the `PACKAGES` file of
  a binary R package repository: the R version, the platform, the time
  of the build and the OS type, separated by a semicolon and a space,
  e.g.
  `R 4.7.0; x86_64-pc-linux-gnu; 2026-10-19 13:19:53 UTC; unix`.
- `linkingto`: empty for source tarballs and for packages without
  `LinkingTo` dependencies. Otherwise the source versions of the
  `LinkingTo` dependencies the binary was built against, as a
  comma-separated list of `<package>@<version>=<id>` entries,
  where `<id>` is the `Id` of that dependency
  version:

  ```
  cpp11@0.5.4=6e0053ce…,systemfonts@1.3.2=828a1780…,textshaping@1.0.5=12209d55…
  ```

  This list is the transitive closure of `LinkingTo` dependencies, not
  a copy of the package's `LinkingTo` field. E.g. ragg has
  `LinkingTo: systemfonts, textshaping`, and its list also includes
  cpp11, because systemfonts and textshaping link to it.
- `yanked`: `NA` if the build is not yanked. Otherwise the time of the
  yank, in RFC 3339 format, see
  [Yanked versions and builds](#yanked-versions-and-builds). Always
  `NA` for source tarballs.
- `yanked_reason`: `NA` if the build is not yanked. Otherwise a
  description of why the build was yanked, for people. It must not
  contain tabs or newlines.

Rules for readers:

- Skip the comment lines, starting with `#`, at the beginning of the
  file.

- Find columns by their name in the header, not by their position.
  New columns may be added later, and the repository may add columns
  that this tidyup does not define. Readers must ignore the columns
  they do not know. The `linkingto`, `sha256`, `md5`, `filesize`,
  `built`, `yanked` and `yanked_reason` columns are optional. An index
  may have `sha256`, `md5`, both, or neither. An index without a
  `yanked` column has no yanked builds.

- In the `sha256`, `md5`, `filesize`, `built`, `yanked` and
  `yanked_reason` columns a missing value is the string `NA`. Clients
  cannot check the download of a file if both `sha256` and `md5` are
  missing.

- Several rows may have the same `version`, `platform` and
  `r_version`. This happens when a package was rebuilt because a
  `LinkingTo` dependency changed, and the `linkingto` column is what
  tells them apart. A client that picks a binary for a lock file needs
  to pick the row whose `linkingto` versions match the versions it
  resolved, or fall back to the source tarball.

- A package without an index, e.g. a Bioconductor package in the CRAN
  repository, has no file, so an HTTP(S) server returns 404.

There is no index of all binaries, and no listing of the `binaries/`
directory. Clients download the indices of the packages they need, one
request per package.

### Yanked versions and builds

A repository can yank a source package version or a single binary
build, e.g. because it is broken. A yanked file is still served, so
lock files that already have it keep working, but clients do not pick
it when they solve dependencies or create a lock file. This is
different from `Blocked`: a blocked version is not served at all.

- A version is yanked with the `Yanked` and `YankedReason` fields of
  its record in `ALLPACKAGES`. The fields are per record, so if the
  same `(Package, Version)` pair has more than one record, e.g.
  because the upstream repository replaced the tarball, each of them
  can be yanked on its own.

- A binary build is yanked with the `yanked` and `yanked_reason`
  columns of its row in the binary index. Source rows are never yanked
  in the binary index, readers check `Yanked` in `ALLPACKAGES` for
  that. If a version is yanked, all its builds are yanked as well,
  and the repository does not need to mark them one by one.

- To yank a whole package, the repository yanks all its versions. A
  package that must not be used at all is `Blocked: package` instead.

- To undo a yank, the repository removes the fields, or sets the
  columns to `NA`.

A missing `Yanked` field or `yanked` value means the version or build
is not yanked.

Rules for readers:

- When solving dependencies, skip yanked versions, unless the
  requirement asks for exactly that version, or the version is already
  in the lock file that is being updated. If only yanked versions
  satisfy a requirement, fail and show `YankedReason`.

- When picking a binary, skip yanked builds. Use another build of the
  same version with matching `linkingto` versions, or fall back to the
  source tarball.

- When updating a lock file, keep the yanked versions that are already
  in it, but tell the user, with the reason. Replace the yanked builds
  that are in it, as above.

- Ignore the time of the yank when hiding newer versions, e.g. with
  `--exclude-newer <date>`: a yanked version is skipped even if it was
  yanked after `<date>`.

Installing packages from a lock file does not need the extended
metadata, so yanks have no effect there: a locked yanked version or
build is installed as it is. A client may offer a separate command
that reads the metadata and reports the yanked versions and builds of
a lock file.

### Platforms

A platform is `source` or a target triple. The platforms are the same
as in `rproj.lock`, see [Tidyup 11](011-rproj-lock.md), so a client can
match the rows of a binary index to the targets of a lock file by
comparing strings.

| Platform | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `aarch64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-apple-darwin` | macOS. |
| `x86_64-w64-mingw32`, `aarch64-w64-mingw32` | Windows. |
| `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-manylinux_<major>_<minor>` | Any x86_64 Linux with glibc `<major>.<minor>` or later, e.g. `manylinux_2_28`. The binaries do not depend on the libraries of a Linux distribution. |
| `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-<distro>-<version>` | A specific Linux distribution and release, e.g. `ubuntu-24.04`, `debian-12`, `rhel-9`, `opensuse-15.6`. |

The architecture is `x86_64` or `aarch64`, never `amd64` or `arm64`.
The `aarch64` forms of the Linux platforms have the same meaning for
ARM64 machines.

The macOS platforms do not have a macOS version. macOS binaries must
work on the same macOS versions as CRAN's macOS binaries for the same
R version and architecture, i.e. their minimum macOS version is the
same as CRAN's. A repository that cannot build binaries for that
macOS version does not serve macOS binaries.

`<distro>` and `<version>` come from the `/etc/os-release` file of the
system the binaries are built for: `<distro>` is the `ID` field, and
`<version>` is the part of `VERSION_ID` that binaries of the
distribution are compatible within: the major version for `rhel`
and `debian`, e.g. `rhel-9`, `major.minor` for `ubuntu` and
`opensuse`, e.g. `ubuntu-24.04`. openSUSE Leap is `opensuse`, not
`opensuse-leap`. With this rule a repository can add
a new distribution without a change to this specification, and a
client can find the platform of the machine from `/etc/os-release`.

A distribution that uses the binaries of another one has that one's
name, e.g. Rocky Linux 9.4 and AlmaLinux 9.4 are `rhel-9`. Which
distributions use the binaries of which other ones is up to the
clients, this tidyup does not list them. The `ID_LIKE` field of
`/etc/os-release` helps, but it is not always enough, e.g. SUSE Linux
Enterprise 15.7 may use the `opensuse-15.6` binaries.

The generic Linux builds follow the `manylinux` naming of Python's
[PEP 600](https://peps.python.org/pep-0600/): `manylinux_2_28`
binaries need glibc 2.28 or later, and do not link to other system
libraries, except the ones that every glibc Linux has. `manylinux` is
not a distribution `ID`, so the two forms do not clash. A machine
with glibc `<major>.<minor>` can use every `manylinux_<x>_<y>` build
with `<x>.<y>` up to its own glibc version, comparing the parts as
integers. A client should prefer a build for the machine's own
distribution and release, and otherwise the `manylinux` build with
the highest glibc version it can use.

Readers must accept platforms they do not know, and skip their rows.
A possible later addition is `<arch>-unknown-linux-musl-musllinux_<major>_<minor>`
for Alpine Linux, also from PEP 600.

### Versioning

The format version has two parts, `<major>.<minor>`, both
non-negative integers, e.g. `1.0`. Readers compare the parts as
integers, so `1.10` is newer than `1.9`. A repository gives the
version in the `Format-Version` field of `METADATA`, and in a
`# Format-Version: <major>.<minor>` comment at the start of every
`ALLPACKAGES`, `ARCHIVEDPACKAGES` and binary index file. All of these
have the same version. This tidyup specifies version 1.0.

Changes that old readers can still read increase the minor version:
new fields in the DCF files, new columns in the binary indices, new
`Blocked` values. The minor version tells readers which fields and
columns the repository knows about. E.g. if a later minor version adds
a field, a missing field in a file of that version means that the field
does not apply to the record, but in a file of an older version it
means that the repository does not provide it.

Changes that old readers cannot read increase the major version and
reset the minor version to zero. The repository serves the new major
version under a new base URL, so it can serve the old and the new
versions side by side, and old clients keep working. E.g. the P3M
instances serve version 1 under `https://ppm.r-pkg.org/v1`, and would
serve version 2 under `https://ppm.r-pkg.org/v2`.

Rules for readers:

- If the major version is one they do not know, readers must refuse
  the files.

- If the minor version is newer than the one they know, readers must
  read the files, and ignore the fields, columns and values they do
  not know. They may warn the user.

- Readers should check the version in each data file as well, not only
  in `METADATA`, because caches may serve files from different updates
  together.

## Implementations

### Server

The CRAN and Bioconductor instances are generated from P3M data and
updated daily. They serve version 1.0 of the format.

This table maps every P3M platform with binaries to the platforms of
this tidyup. `<arch>` is `x86_64` or `aarch64`, P3M has `aarch64`
binaries for `macos`, `manylinux_2_28`, `noble`, `resolute`, `rhel9`
and `rhel10`, and `x86_64` binaries for all of them.

| P3M platform | Platform |
|---|---|
| `macos` | `<arch>-apple-darwin` |
| `windows` | `x86_64-w64-mingw32` |
| `manylinux_2_28` | `<arch>-unknown-linux-gnu-manylinux_2_28` |
| `xenial` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-ubuntu-16.04` |
| `bionic` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-ubuntu-18.04` |
| `focal` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-ubuntu-20.04` |
| `jammy` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-ubuntu-22.04` |
| `noble` | `<arch>-unknown-linux-gnu-ubuntu-24.04` |
| `resolute` | `<arch>-unknown-linux-gnu-ubuntu-26.04` |
| `bullseye` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-debian-11` |
| `bookworm` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-debian-12` |
| `trixie` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-debian-13` |
| `centos7` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-rhel-7` |
| `centos8` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-rhel-8` |
| `rhel9` | `<arch>-unknown-linux-gnu-rhel-9` |
| `rhel10` | `<arch>-unknown-linux-gnu-rhel-10` |
| `opensuse42` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-opensuse-42.3` |
| `opensuse15` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-opensuse-15.0` |
| `opensuse152` ... `opensuse156` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-opensuse-15.2` ... `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-opensuse-15.6` |

P3M also has build targets that reuse the binaries of another one:
`rhel7` and `rhel8` use `centos7` and `centos8`, and the SUSE Linux
Enterprise targets use the openSUSE Leap binaries, e.g. `sles157` uses
`opensuse156`. These are not separate platforms. A client on CentOS 7,
or on SLES 15.7, finds the matching platform the same way as on Rocky
Linux, see [Platforms](#platforms).

### `rig`

`rig` uses the extended metadata for:

- solving dependencies, using all versions in `ALLPACKAGES`, not just
  the current ones;
- `--exclude-newer <date>`: hiding the versions with a `Snapshot`
  date after `<date>`;
- listing available packages, hiding archived packages, and telling the
  user when a package was archived;
- picking binaries for each target of a lock file, matching `platform`,
  `r_version` and `linkingto`;
- skipping yanked versions and builds when it solves and locks;
- recording `Id` in the lock file and in installed
  packages, to tell whether an installed package is the same as the
  locked one.

## Backwards compatibility

The extended metadata is served in addition to the regular
repository, under a different URL. Existing tools are not affected.

## How to teach

Users will not see these files.

## Unresolved questions

None currently.

## Alternatives

### Per-day `PACKAGES` files

P3M already serves a full `PACKAGES` file for every day. A client
could download these, but finding all versions of a package, or the
first snapshot of a version, would need thousands of downloads.

### An index of all binaries

A single file listing every binary of every package would be very
large for CRAN (cli alone has over 3,000 rows), and almost all of it
would be irrelevant for any one project. One small file per package means
a client only downloads what it needs, and the requests can run in
parallel.

### JSON instead of DCF and TSV

JSON would be easier to parse with general tools, but DCF is what R
and existing R tools already read, and `ALLPACKAGES` is a valid
`PACKAGES` file. TSV keeps the binary indices small and fast to parse.
